context_blurb:
Four times in the last century, researchers defied what most experts believed, and the evidence proved them right; once it proved a bold claim wrong. Each time the doubters had real reasons. And each time a test that other scientists could check settled it.

In Western Australia the pathologist Robin Warren kept finding spiral bacteria in inflamed stomach lining, and the young doctor Barry Marshall joined him. Ulcers were blamed on worry and acid, and with reason: stomach acid kills nearly every germ swallowed, and a 1954 study had found none of these bacteria in stomach samples. In 1984, with piglets failing to catch the germ, Marshall swallowed a broth of the bacteria himself. Ten days on, a camera on a tube and a snip of tissue showed gastritis: an inflamed lining, with the bacteria in it. It was no ulcer, but his paper argued that a lasting infection prepares the way for one. In a trial of a hundred infected patients with ulcers just past the stomach, far fewer ulcers came back within a year where the bacteria were cleared: 21 in every 100, against 84 where they stayed. Marshall and Warren shared the 2005 Nobel Prize. Marshall said everyone had been against him; others say his doubters showed proper scepticism until such evidence arrived.

In 1982 Dan Shechtman aimed electrons at an aluminium-manganese alloy and counted a ring of ten bright spots. Textbooks defined a crystal as a solid whose atoms repeat one small pattern over and over, and geometry forbids any repeating pattern to have tenfold symmetry, just as regular pentagons cannot tile a floor. Shape was never the test: a metal's tiny grains are crystals without flat faces. Linus Pauling, a double Nobel winner, blamed twinning, the crystallographers' standard answer: several normal crystals joined at angles, their spots adding into a pattern that none makes alone. But Shechtman had squeezed his beam onto one tiny grain, and that single grain gave the whole tenfold pattern. Other labs confirmed the patterns, Pauling held out until his death in 1994, and in 1992 crystallographers redefined a crystal as any solid giving a clear-cut pattern of spots; Shechtman's Nobel Prize came in 2011.

In 1967 Lynn Margulis argued that mitochondria and chloroplasts, small parts inside animal and plant cells, began as swallowed bacteria; over a dozen journals had rejected her paper. Critics wanted firmer evidence, and a cell might have built these parts from within. A cell gets more mitochondria only when old ones grow and split in two, as bacteria do; if it loses them all, it can never make more. By 1982 Michael Gray, Ford Doolittle and others had found chloroplast DNA closest to that of cyanobacteria, bacteria that make food from sunlight. Mitochondrial DNA soon matched oxygen-using bacteria, and most biologists were won over. Her third claim, that flagella, the whip-like tails some cells swim with, came from spiral bacteria, failed the same kind of test: flagella have no DNA of their own at all.

In 1923 J Harlen Bretz proposed that one sudden, giant flood had cut eastern Washington's Channeled Scablands. For a century geology had explained the land by slow, everyday change instead of Noah's Flood, so a sudden catastrophe seemed a step back. Critics also asked where so much water could have come from, and for years he could not say. In 1940 Joseph Pardee showed that huge gravel ridges on the floor of Montana's vanished, ice-dammed Glacial Lake Missoula are giant current ripples. Only a deep, fast torrent builds ripples that size: the ice dam had failed, and the lake had emptied in a sudden rush. Geologists now count forty or more such floods, so Bretz was right about the kind of event, not the number. He won the Geological Society of America's Penrose Medal in 1979.

Not every bold claim wins. In 1989 the noted electrochemist Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons announced that a palladium rod in heavy water, whose hydrogen is a heavier kind, gave off more heat under an electric current than chemistry could explain. They credited it to nuclear fusion, though fusion in the Sun needs some 15 million degrees. Labs around the world found no extra heat and no sign of fusion, and fusion making that much heat would have given off neutrons deadly to the experimenters. Energy Department reviews in 1989 and 2004 found no convincing evidence. Other scientists could repeat the earlier tests; no one else could get this result.
